items.question: A malloc-heavy hot loop reports mean 45 ns and p50 41 ns, yet p99 is about a microsecond. Without notes: which mechanism produced that p99 in lesson 01's lab, what does fresh heap memory consist of before its first write, and what are the other two ways a general-purpose allocator hurts the tail?
key: First-touch page faults: fresh heap memory is only address space, and the first write to each page takes a page fault (the kernel's cost, not malloc's); in the lab one allocation in 64 paid it (16 KiB page / 256 B).
Locks / arenas: a shared allocator must synchronise threads (glibc creates extra arenas when it detects mutex contention).
Scattered nodes: node containers spread over the heap and cost cache misses on every walk.

items.question: New setting: an audit-log thread on an x86-64 Linux box (4 KiB pages) allocates a fresh 4 KiB buffer with `new` for every record and keeps every buffer for the whole session. Roughly how many of its allocations pay a page fault, compared with the 1-in-64 you saw in lesson 01, and what removes those faults from the logging path?
key: About one fault per record (every allocation lands on at least one untouched page), versus 1 in 64 when 256 B objects shared a 16 KiB page: the ratio is page size / object size.
The cost is first touch by the kernel, so a faster malloc does not fix it.

Fix: take the memory from a region that was pre-faulted (touched) at start-up, for example an hft::thread_arena (warmed) or reused buffers from a pool, so no fresh page is first touched in the hot path.

items.question: From memory: which two declarations move a thread's containers onto hft_mem, how does `hft::allocator` find the arena when the container stores no resource pointer, and where does an erased node go?
key: `hft::thread_arena arena;` once, at the top of the thread that owns the data, then an alias such as `hft::map<K, V>` (or hft::unordered_map, flat_map, vector, string, multi_index ...).
hft::allocator is an empty class that reads a thread_local pointer set by the thread_arena constructor.
An erased node goes back to the pool's free list and the next same-size insert reuses it, so churn calls no operator new.

items.question: New setting: a risk thread keeps `std::unordered_map<long, std::vector<long>>` (account id to open-order ids, at most 64 per account); accounts are added and removed all day. Make the whole structure come from that thread's arena with no global operator new in the hot loop. Give the type, and the two things needed beyond swapping the outer type.
key: Create `hft::thread_arena` first on the risk thread; type `hft::unordered_map<long, hft::vector<long>>`.
The inner type must be hft too: a std::vector inside would still take its buffer from operator new (the nested-type trap).
The inner vectors grow by reallocating, which a pool does not prevent: reserve(64) when each is created (or use static_vector<long, 64>, which never allocates).

items.question: Name the two hft_mem switches that turn a hidden hot-path allocation into a failure. For each, say when it takes effect and what it still allows, and name the standard resource both are built on.
key: `arena.seal()` at run time, after warm-up: the pool may still recycle blocks it owns, but any request for new memory (refill, flat-container growth) throws std::bad_alloc.
`-DHFT_MEM_TRIPWIRE=1` at build time: when the region is full, throw instead of silently falling back to malloc.
Both use std::pmr::null_memory_resource(), whose allocate always throws std::bad_alloc.

items.question: New setting: a CI replay of a full trading day fails with std::bad_alloc after `arena.seal()`. The stack shows `push_back` on an `hft::vector<Fill>` that was never reserved. What does the failure tell you, what is the fix, and what would the same code do in a production build without seal() or the tripwire?
key: The vector grew in the hot path: growth requests a new, bigger block (new memory), which a sealed arena forbids.
Fix: reserve() it to its maximum size during warm-up, before seal().
Production without seal or tripwire: the growth succeeds silently (from the arena, or from malloc once the region is full), so it shows up as a latency spike, not an error.

items.question: Predict, layer by layer, for the chain `unsynchronized_pool_resource pool(&mono)` over `monotonic_buffer_resource mono(buf, sizeof buf, null_memory_resource())`: (a) a node is deallocated, (b) the next same-size allocate, (c) the pool later needs a new chunk after buf is used up.
key: (a) The pool takes the block back on its size-class free list; the monotonic layer is not involved (its deallocate is a no-op anyway).
(b) The pool hands back that freed block; no upstream call.
(c) The pool asks mono for a chunk, mono is out of buffer and asks its upstream, null_memory_resource(), which throws std::bad_alloc.

items.question: New setting (not trading): a web server's JSON parser needs per-request scratch from a 64 KiB stack buffer, spilling to the normal heap if a request is bigger, all freed in one step when the request ends. Which std::pmr resource, with which upstream, and which call at the end of each request? Why is no pool needed?
key: `std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource scratch(buf, sizeof buf, std::pmr::new_delete_resource())` (or the default upstream, which is new_delete initially).
Call `release()` at the end of each request (or destroy the resource).
No pool: nothing is freed individually during a request, everything dies together, and a monotonic resource's deallocate is a no-op.

items.question: From memory: when is each the right choice, and what is the catch you saw in the lab: `boost::container::static_vector<T, N>`, `small_vector<T, N>`, and `boost::pool<>`?
key: static_vector: hard, small upper bound; never allocates. Catch: on overflow it throws boost::container::bad_alloc, which `catch (const std::bad_alloc&)` did not catch here.
small_vector: keeps N elements inline, then uses its allocator.
boost::pool<>: one hot fixed-size object type you own; one block size, no lock (2 ns per allocate+free pair here, the fastest row).

items.question: New setting (not trading): a telemetry module may not allocate after boot. It keeps at most 32 readings per sensor in `boost::container::static_vector<Reading, 32>` and guards overflow with `try { r.push_back(x); } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { drop(x); }`. A field report says a 33rd reading crashed the process. Explain, and fix the guard.
key: static_vector throws boost::container::bad_alloc on overflow, and that is not a std::bad_alloc here, so the catch clause does not match and the exception escapes.
Fix: check `r.size() < r.capacity()` before push_back, or catch boost::container::bad_alloc (or a broader base you have verified it derives from).

items.question: A reviewer's bump-region `memory_resource` returns `nullptr` from do_allocate when the region is full, and its do_is_equal is `return true;`. Name both bugs and the rule each breaks.
key: do_allocate must throw (std::bad_alloc) when storage of the requested size and alignment cannot be obtained, never return null.

do_is_equal may be true only if memory from one resource can be deallocated through the other; a region can free only its own memory, so `this == &other`. Always-true lets containers (move, swap) ask region A to free region B's blocks: memory corruption.

items.question: New setting: a bump resource over a 1 MiB staging buffer handed over by a device driver (base address 4 KiB-aligned), `off_` starting at 0. Requests: 1 byte with alignment 1, then 64 bytes with alignment 256. At which offsets do they land and what is `off_` after each? Where would the second land if you forgot the rounding line?
key: First: offset 0, off_ = 1.
Without rounding it lands at offset 1: a misaligned pointer (address % 256 = 1), which the caller assumed was 256-aligned.

items.question: Explain WHY the NUMA start-up order is pin, mmap, mbind, touch, hot path: what each later step needs from an earlier one. Then give the one-call libnuma alternative and why it belongs at start-up only.
key: mbind needs the mapped range, so mmap comes first; mbind affects only new allocations, so it must precede the touch; the first touch picks the node, so the thread is pinned before touching; the hot path starts after the pages exist.
`numa_alloc_onnode(size, node)`: relatively slow compared with malloc, rounded up to the page size, must be freed with numa_free(); so call it once at start-up, never in the hot path.

items.question: New setting (not trading): a database on a two-socket Linux box allocates and zeroes its whole buffer pool from the start-up thread on socket 0, then starts query threads on both sockets. Queries on socket 1 are slower. Diagnose, give two ways to verify it, and the fix.
key: The start-up thread touched every page first, so under the default local policy all pages sit on node 0; socket-1 threads read remote memory.
Verify with any two of: `numastat -p <pid>`, the N<node>=<pages> fields in /proc/<pid>/numa_maps, move_pages() with nodes NULL (returns each page's node).
Fix: one pool per node, mapped (and mbind-ed) and first touched by a thread pinned on that node, used by that node's threads.

items.question: Why must memory that hft_mem handed out on one thread be freed on that same thread? Say what the checked build and an unchecked build do when another thread frees it, and the safe pattern.
key: The allocator finds the arena through the current thread's thread_local pointer, so a free on thread B goes to B's arena, which does not own the block.
Checked build: abort with "deallocate of memory that is not from this thread's arena" (exit 134 in the lab); unchecked: the wrong pool is corrupted.
Safe pattern: send the object (or the request to free it) back to the owning thread, for example through a queue; never free into a pool on another node.

items.question: New setting: a config-reload thread builds a fresh `hft::map<Sym, Limit>` and moves it to the risk thread, which destroys the previous map at the next reload. Name what goes wrong (two cases, depending on whether the reload thread's arena still exists) and give a fix.
key: The map's nodes live in the reload thread's arena; destroying the map on the risk thread frees them into the risk thread's arena: checked build aborts (not from this thread's arena), unchecked corrupts the wrong pool.
If the reload thread's arena has already been destroyed, its region is unmapped and the destructor crashes walking the nodes (SIGSEGV, like the outlive trap).

Fix: let the owning (risk) thread build its own map from data it receives, or return containers to their owning thread for destruction; for truly shared structures use a synchronized resource or redesign to one owner.

items.question: From lesson 04's locality bench (two maps filled interleaved, walk map A with random keys): rank default malloc, one shared pool, and a pool per container, and explain why the shared pool came last.
key: Pool per container fastest (about 13 ns/node), default malloc next (about 17), one shared pool slowest (about 26).
A shared pool interleaves A's and B's nodes (A B A B), so walking A touches about twice the memory; a per-container pool keeps A's nodes adjacent.

items.question: New setting (not trading): a physics simulation stores 1,000,000 particles as a 128 B struct, and the per-frame collision pass reads only the 3 position fields. What layout change would you try first, what direction and rough size of effect does lesson 04's measurement suggest, and why?
key: A hot/cold split: keep the hot position fields in their own compact array and the rest elsewhere.
In lesson 04 scanning 3 hot fields from a 24 B array cost about 10x less per element than from inside a 128 B struct (0.41 vs 4.04 ns); re-measure on the target machine.
Why: the scan touches far fewer bytes and cache lines per element.

items.question: Explain how a hand-maintained state enum and an intrusive hook can disagree about whether an order is pending-send, which one is right, and why the hook cannot drift.
key: A code path links the order into the list but forgets to update the enum (lab: "state says PendingSend? 0, send hook says linked? 1").
The hook is right: being linked IS being in the list (safe_link resets the hook on erase), so there is no second copy of the truth to forget.

items.question: New setting (not trading): a ride-hailing dispatcher keeps drivers in three lists, idle, en-route and on-trip, and every driver is in exactly one. Design the hooks and fields so that "which state is driver D in?" is O(1) and correct, "in two states at once" cannot happen, and a state change allocates nothing.
key: One hook shared by the three state lists: a hook can be in only one container, so two states at once is unrepresentable; moving is unlink then push_back, O(1), no allocation (drivers live in a slab).
is_linked() only says "in some list", so add a 1-byte state tag (updated with each move) to say which; or give each list its own hook (exact, 16 B each), which makes two-at-once representable again.

items.question: Give the cost of each in Boost.Intrusive: (a) erasing a known order from a default bi::list, (b) find by id in an intrusive set, (c) erase(it) from an intrusive unordered_set, (d) slist::erase(it), (e) size() with constant_time_size<false>, (f) destroying a safe_link list of n elements. Which of these allocate?
key: (a) O(1) given the object (iterator_to / s_iterator_to), but it needs the list object for its size counter; (b) O(log n).
(c) average O(1), worst O(size): buckets are singly linked, so erase must find the predecessor; (d) linear in the elements before it.
(e) O(n); (f) O(n): it unlinks every element.
None allocates: intrusive containers allocate nothing.

items.question: New setting (not trading): an editor keeps its undo history in a `bi::slist` (push_front for each edit) and often removes an arbitrary edit by iterator. Profiling shows removal gets slower as the history grows. Why, and what change makes removal O(1)? What does that change cost per edit?
key: slist::erase(it) is linear in the elements before it: a singly linked node does not know its predecessor, so erase walks to it.
Switch to a doubly linked bi::list (erase via iterator_to / s_iterator_to is O(1)); the hook grows from 8 B to 16 B per edit.

items.question: State the teardown rules for a slab and the intrusive lists that link its objects: declaration order, what must happen before an object is destroyed, and what a safe_link list's destructor does that a normal_link one does not, with its measured cost.
key: Declare the slab (owner) before the containers, so it is destroyed after them.
Unlink every object before destroying it (erase_and_dispose / clear_and_dispose with a disposer that calls the slab's destroy); the container never owns anything.
A safe_link list's destructor unlinks every element, linear in n (about 1.4 ms for 1,000,000 orders here); normal_link takes about 0 but leaves every hook holding links into a dead list.

items.question: New setting (not trading): a network proxy keeps `Conn` objects in an `hft::slab<Conn>` and links idle ones into `idle` (a bi::list). A cleanup pass must free every idle connection older than T. Write the one call, and say what happens if instead you call `slab.destroy(&c)` inside `for (Conn& c : idle)`.
key: `idle.remove_and_dispose_if([&](const Conn& c) { return c.age > T; }, [&](Conn* c) { slab.destroy(c); });` (the disposer runs after the element is removed).

Destroy inside the range-for destroys a linked object: the safe_link hook asserts in a debug build (exit 134); with NDEBUG the slot is reused and the program crashes later; erasing inside a range-for also crashes because the loop's ++ follows a reset (null) link. Use `it = l.erase(it)` or remove_and_dispose_if.

items.question: Describe lesson 07's intrusive LRU: what a hit does, what a miss does when full, how keys are looked up, and the final contents after accesses 1,2,3,1,4,5 with capacity 3.
key: Hit: unlink the entry and push_back it (the back is most recently used); miss when full: evict front().
Key lookup: an intrusive unordered_set with key_of_value on the same object.
1,2,3,1,4,5 evicts 2, then 3, leaving 1 4 5.

items.question: New setting (not trading): a web session store must expire sessions idle for 30 minutes, checked once a second; most sessions are touched many times before they expire. Sketch an intrusive-over-a-slab design: structure, what a touch does, what the expiry check does, and their costs.
key: Sessions in a slab, linked into one intrusive list in last-touch order, plus an id index (hash map or intrusive unordered_set) to find them.
Touch: unlink + push_back, O(1), no allocation, so the front is always the least recently touched (the pending-ack / LRU pattern).
Expiry: look only at front() and pop while it is older than 30 minutes (disposing to the slab); no scan of live sessions. (A timer wheel is also acceptable if it handles rescheduling on touch.)

items.question: Name four situations in which lesson 07's verdict says intrusive + slab is the wrong choice, and what to use in the first one.
key: The object lives in one structure only: a reserved flat_map or vector is smaller and scans faster (375 vs 875 ns per 1,024 lean vs hooked orders).
Lookup by key dominates and membership changes are rare: multi_index is safer at a measured cost.
Objects cross threads or outlive their lists (nobody owns them).
A public API (Boost's own advice).

items.question: New setting: a colleague proposes intrusive lists over a slab for an exchange's reference-data table: 30,000 instruments loaded at start of day, looked up by symbol millions of times, never moved between structures, read by several threads. Give your verdict and the reasons, and what you would use instead.
key: Verdict: intrusive is the wrong choice here: each instrument sits in one structure and never changes membership, so intrusive's strength (O(1) membership changes across several lists) is unused.

Lookup by key dominates (use a keyed container, e.g. a reserved flat or hash map, or multi_index if several keys), and objects are shared across threads, where intrusive lifetimes are the user's problem.
A contiguous, reserved container is also smaller and faster to scan than hooked objects.
